verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：摩押三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去她的刑罚；因为她将以东王的骸骨焚烧成灰。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because Moab has committed three crimes[NOTE:1]—make that four[NOTE:2]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:3] They burned the bones of Edom’s king into lime.[NOTE:4]
notes: Traditionally, “transgressions” (KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV) or “sins” (NIV). For an explanation of the atrocities outlined in this oracle as treaty violations of God’s mandate to Noah in Gen 9:5-7, see the note on the word “violations” in 1:3.
Heb “Because of three violations of Moab, even because of four.”sn On the three…four style that introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2 see the note on the word “four” in 1:3.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The translation understands the pronominal object to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. For another option see the note on the word “judgment” in 1:3.

The Moabites apparently desecrated the tomb of an Edomite king and burned his bones into a calcined substance which they then used as plaster (cf. Deut 27:2, 4). See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 72. Receiving a proper burial was very important in this culture. Desecrating a tomb or a deceased individual’s bones was considered an especially heinous act.
verses.commentary:
2:1 The literary judgment form (i.e. funeral dirge) of chapter one continues through chapter two (cf. Amos 1:3; see notes there).

▣ "Moab" These were also relatives of the Israelis through Lot (cf. Gen. 19:30-38). The
country is in the trans-jordan area just north of Edom between the Arnon and Zered Rivers.

SPECIAL TOPIC: MOAB

▣ "because he burned the bones of the king of Moab to lime" These actions, of which we have no biblical or
archaeological information, involved

- opening the grave

- removing the remains

- burning them

- mixing them to make mortar (i.e. for buildings) or plaster (i.e. for whitewashing walls)

These actions were seen as a way to humiliate and to affect negatively one's place/rest in the afterlife
(i.e. 2 Kgs. 23:16-20; Isa. 33:12). This purposeful violation of that which was culturally sacred and taboo shows the level of animosity.
This does not refer to cremation as a way of disposing of a dead body, but to a later desecration! It does, however, give
me a chance to discuss modern concerns about cremation (see Special Topic below).

Cremation was an abominable practice to all the Near Eastern people. It is only mentioned
in the Bible in connection with great crimes (cf. Gen. 28:24; Lev. 20:14; 21:9; Josh. 7:15,25). Apparently out of
hatred Moab burned the king of Edom's bones and mixed them with mortar to build buildings or plaster to
whitewash walls (Targums). Lime (BDB 966, cf. Isa. 33:12) was an ingredient of mortar and plaster (whitewash).

It is possible that this act is imagery for complete destruction (i.e. Vulgate). It is difficult
to interpret VERBS that have both literal and figurative uses. This is especially true of
poetic passages, as the book of Amos.

The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT), p. 766, mentions that the only piece of information
about this general period comes from the Mesha Inscription. The problem is this relates to the 9th century
B.C. and our current text is related to the 8th century B.C. The Assyrian King
Tiglath-Pileser conquered thie transJordan area in 734 B.C.

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF ASSYRIA, #19

SPECIAL TOPIC: BURIAL PRACTICES

SPECIAL TOPIC: CREMATION

verses.zh: 我却要降火在摩押，烧灭加略的宫殿。摩押必在哄嚷呐喊吹角之中死亡。
verses.en: So I will set Moab on fire,[NOTE:1] and it will consume Kerioth’s[NOTE:2] fortresses.Moab will perish[NOTE:3] in the heat of battle[NOTE:4] amid war cries and the blaring[NOTE:5] of the ram’s horn.[NOTE:6]
notes: The destruction of Moab by fire is an example of a judgment in kind—as the Moabites committed the crime of “burning,” so the Lord will punish them by setting them on fire.
Kerioth was an important Moabite city. See Jer 48:24, 41.
Or “die” (KJV, NASB, NRSV, TEV); cf. NAB “shall meet death.”
Or “in the tumult.” This word refers to the harsh confusion of sounds that characterized an ancient battle—a mixture of war cries, shouts, shrieks of pain, clashes of weapons, etc.
Heb “sound” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV).
The ram’s horn (used as a trumpet) was blown to signal the approaching battle.
verses.commentary:
2:2 "I will send fire" This phrase refers to

- YHWH's judgment

- the literal burning of cities

It is a recurrent phrase in Amos 1:4,7,10,12,14; 2:2,5 and Hosea 8:14. Fire is often sent as

- a cleansing agent

- a symbol of God's presence

- a means of judgment

SPECIAL TOPIC: FIRE

▣ "the citadels" See note at Amos 1:4.

▣ "Kerioth" This (BDB 90, KB 1142) is a region's or city's name. The NEB, following the LXX, translated it
as "towns" (because of the DEFINITIVE ARTICLE, cf. Jer. 48:41), but the revision of the
NEB, called the REB, puts the place name back into the translation (i.e. "the palaces of Kerioth"). This
city is also mentioned in Jer. 48:24,41. This city (possibly Kir, cf. Isa. 15:1) had a major shrine to
the Moabite fertility god, Chemosh (cf. The Mesha Stone L.12; 1 Kgs. 11:33).

The UBS Text Project, p. 277, gives "Kerioth" a "B" rating. The difference is only vocalization.

SPECIAL TOPIC: CHEMOSH

▣ "with war cries" See note at Amos 1:14. War cries and trumpet blasts are often used
as signals in battle. The phrase in some contexts refers to the sound of confusion and fear during battle.

▣ "the sound of the trumpet" Trumpets were used to direct troops in the field. See note at Amos 1:14.

SPECIAL TOPIC: HORNS USED BY ISRAEL

verses.zh: 我必剪除摩押中的审判者，将其中的一切首领和他一同杀戮。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: I will remove[NOTE:1] Moab’s leader;[NOTE:2] I will kill all Moab’s[NOTE:3] officials[NOTE:4] with him.”The Lord has spoken!
notes: Heb “cut off” (so KJV, NASB, NRSV); cf. NAB “root out,” NCV “bring to an end.”
Heb “the leader [traditionally, “judge”] from her midst.”
Heb “her”; the referent (Moab) has been specified in the translation for clarity.
Or “princes” (KJV, NAB, NASB, NLT); cf. TEV, CEV “leaders.”
verses.commentary:
2:3 "the judge" This is used in the sense of monarch. The king acted as judge (cf. Micah 5:2), as
God's representative (cf. Gen. 18:25; Jdg. 11:27; Ps. 50:6; 75:7; 94:2; Isa. 33:22). The parallel phrase, "all her
princes," refers to the royal family. Moab will be totally destroyed as a nation (cf. Mal. 1:2-5).

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：犹大人三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去他们的刑罚；因为他们厌弃耶和华的训诲，不遵守他的律例。他们列祖所随从虚假的偶像使他们走迷了。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because Judah has committed three covenant transgressions[NOTE:1]—make that four[NOTE:2]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:3] They rejected the Lord’s law;[NOTE:4] they did not obey his commands.Their false gods,[NOTE:5] to which their fathers were loyal,[NOTE:6] led them astray.
notes: This is the same Hebrew term that is translated “crimes” in the previous oracles (see at 1:3). The change to “covenant transgressions” reflects the probability that the prophet is condemning the nation of Israel for violating stipulations of the Mosaic Law.
Heb “Because of three violations of Judah, even because of four.”sn On the three…four style that introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2 see the note on the word “four” in 1:3.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The translation understands the pronominal object to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. For another option see the note on the word “judgment” in 1:3.
Or “instruction”; cf. NCV “teachings.”

Heb “lies.” This may very well be a derogatory term for idols (perhaps also at Ps 40:4 ET [40:5 HT]). Elsewhere false gods are called “vanities” (Deut 32:21; 1 Kgs 16:13, 26) and a delusion (Isa 66:3). In no other prophetic passages, however, are they called “lies.” The term could refer to the deceptions of false prophets (note Ezek 13:6-9; cf. Hab 2:3). See F. I. Andersen and D. N. Freedman, Amos (AB), 301-6.

Heb “after which their fathers walked.” The expression “to walk after” is an idiom meaning “to be loyal to.” See S. M. Paul, Amos (Hermeneia), 75-76.sn Here the idolatry of the parents carried over to the children, who persisted in worshiping the idols to which their fathers were loyal.
verses.commentary:
2:4 "Judah" The charges against Judah are theological (rejection of YHWH's covenant, i.e. Mosaic Laws)
not just violent acts against other people groups/relatives. The charges would have been denied by Judah, but apparently
the same sins against YHWH which characterized Israel were also committed by Judah (cf. Jer. 3:6-10; Ezek. 23:1-49).

▣ "they rejected the law of the Lord" The VERBAL
"rejected" (BDB 549, KB 540, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT) is used in two seemingly opposite
senses (i.e. conditional covenant, see SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT):

- to reject or refuse someone or something (i.e. here, God's law)

- for God refusing to reject His people. They reject Him and His covenant, prophets, and worship, but
He, the covenant God, punishes them but does not fully reject them.

The paradox is clearly seen in a series of texts from Jer. 6:30; 7:29; 14:19; and 31:37! In
Amos (cf. Amos 2:4; 5:21) and Hosea (cf. Hosea 4:6 [twice]; 9:17) YHWH rejects a generation of His people
because of their willful rejection of Him and His law (cf. Hosea 4:6; 8:1,12)! All of Israel's descendants were
never right with God, only those who exercised faith, repentance, and obedience!

I have come to believe that the longsuffering of YHWH towards the seed of Abraham ended
in A.D. 70 with the Roman destruction of the temple. The Mosaic covenant has been filled and
universalized by the new covenant brought about in Jesus (i.e. Matt. 5:17-20,21-48).

I believe that Jesus' Olivet Discourse (Matt. 24; Mark 13; Luke 17; 21) and Paul's "the man of
lawlessness" (i.e. 2 Thess. 2), as well as the book of Revelation, describes this A.D. 70 "coming" of Jesus.

This view of eschatology is called Partial-Preterism. Please my exegetical, verse-by-verse commentary
on these passages free online.

▣ "law. . .statutes" These are the Hebrew terms

- law ‒ BDB 435

- statutes ‒ BDB 349

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION

▣ "their lies also have led them astray" This term "lies" (BDB 469) means "lie," "falsehood,"
or "deceptive thing." NIDOTTE, vol. 2, p. 619, characterizes it well, "emphasizes an action or word that is
false, a lie, because it somehow violates God's character, word, or deed, as expressed in himself, his prophet
or his creations." Psalm 40:5 and the NIV reflect this concept. The "lies" refer to false teaching and the
worship of false gods (cf. Hab. 2:18).

This same concept is carried over in the NT where in 1 John the "lie" refers to unbelief
in Jesus, the ultimate sin and covenant incompatibility.

SPECIAL TOPIC: IDOLATRY

SPECIAL TOPIC: CONSEQUENCES OF IDOLATRY

▣ "their fathers walked" This is an idiomatic way of asserting that this generation, as well
as previous generations, faithfully worshiped the fertility gods of Canaan (i.e. Ba'al and Asherah/Astarte).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE PATH, THE WAY

SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE

verses.zh: 我却要降火在犹大，烧灭耶路撒冷的宫殿。
verses.en: So I will set Judah on fire,and it will consume Jerusalem’s fortresses.”[NOTE:1]
notes: For the location of Jerusalem see Map5-B1; Map6-F3; Map7-E2; Map8-F2; Map10-B3; JP1-F4; JP2-F4; JP3-F4; JP4-F4.
verses.commentary:
2:5 This is a reference to the Neo-Babylonian Exile that will befall Judah in the days ahead (i.e. 586 B.C.)

SPECIAL TOPIC: KINGS OF NEO-BABYLON, D.

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：以色列人三番四次地犯罪，我必不免去他们的刑罚；因他们为银子卖了义人，为一双鞋卖了穷人。
verses.en: This is what the Lord says:“Because Israel has committed three covenant transgressions[NOTE:1]—make that four[NOTE:2]—I will not revoke my decree of judgment.[NOTE:3] They sold the innocent[NOTE:4] for silver, the needy for a pair of sandals.[NOTE:5]
notes: For this translation see the note at 2:4.

Heb “Because of three violations of Israel, even because of four.”sn On the three…four style that introduces each of the judgment oracles of chaps. 1-2 see the note on the word “four” in 1:3. Only in this last oracle against Israel does one find the list of four specific violations expected based on the use of a similar formula elsewhere in wisdom literature (see Prov 30:18-19, 29-31). This adaptation of the normal pattern indicates the Lord’s focus on Israel here (he is too bent on judging Israel to dwell very long on her neighbors) and emphasizes Israel’s guilt with respect to the other nations (Israel’s list fills up before the others’ lists do). See R. B. Chisholm, “‘For three sins…even for four’: the numerical sayings in Amos,” BSac 147 (1990) 188-97.

Heb “I will not bring it [or “him”] back.” The translation understands the pronominal object to refer to the decree of judgment that follows; the referent (the decree) has been specified in the translation for clarity. For another option see the note on the word “judgment” in 1:3.

Or “honest” (CEV, NLT). The Hebrew word sometimes has a moral-ethical connotation, “righteous, godly,” but the parallelism (note “poor”) suggests a socio-economic or legal sense here. The practice of selling debtors as slaves is in view (Exod 21:2-11; Lev 25:35-55; Deut 15:12-18). See the note at Exod 21:8 and G. C. Chirichigno, Debt-Slavery in Israel and the Ancient Near East (JSOTSup). Probably the only “crime” the victim had committed was being unable to pay back a loan or an exorbitant interest rate on a loan. Some have suggested that this verse refers to bribery in legal proceedings: the innocent are “sold” in the sense that those in power pay off the elders or judges for favorable decisions (5:12; cf. Exod 23:6-7).

Perhaps the expression “for a pair of sandals” indicates a relatively small price or debt. Some suggest that the sandals may have been an outward token of a more substantial purchase price. Others relate the sandals to a ritual attached to the transfer of property, signifying here that the poor would be losing their inherited family lands because of debt (Ruth 4:7; cf. Deut 25:8-10). Still others emend the Hebrew form slightly to נֶעְלָם (neʿlam, “hidden thing”; from the root עָלַם, ʿalam, “to hide”) and understand this as referring to a bribe.
verses.commentary:
2:6 "Israel" Amos got the attention of his audience by first proclaiming judgment against the surrounding enemies,
then their anticipation was hightened by proclaiming judgment on Israel's covenant brothers (Judah), but now he shocked them
by turning to God's judgment on them!

The northern group of tribes that split from the southern group in 922 B.C. was called by several names.

- the northern ten tribes

- Israel (the collective name)

- Samaria (the captial city)

- Ephraim (the largest tribe)

This northern group of tribes included all except

- Judah

- Simeon

- Benjamin

- most Levites

SPECIAL TOPIC: ISRAEL (the name)

▣ "Because they sell the righteous for money" Because of the allusion to the purchase of slaves
by Edom from/to the Philistines (cf. Amos 1:6), and the Phoenicians (cf. Amos 1:9), this is probably a reference to selling their
countrymen into slavery. The term "sell" (BDB 569, KB 581, Qal INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
is used in two senses:

- persons kidnaped to be sold as slaves

- to sell oneself to a creditor for a period of time

It is certain that this is a reference against those who were wealthy, who abused the socially
ostracized and needy (cf. Prov. 14:31; 17:5; Micah 2:1-3).

The term "righteous" here is used in parallel with

- "the needy" (Amos 2:6)

- "the helpless" (Amos 2:7)

- "the humble" (Amos 2:7)

So in this context (and remember context determines meaning) it does not have a theological
orientation, but a social one. Righteous people are related to YHWH and His law and thereby treat their covenant
partners appropriately. Righteousness in Amos has a vertical and a horizontal aspect. In Hosea the term takes
on a more religious (theological or vertical aspect) orientation (cf. Hosea 2:19; 10:12; 14:9. In context it is often
related to hesed (i.e. covenant faithfulness; see
SPECIAL TOPIC: LOVINGKINDNESS).

Because this context has a legal/judicial flavor, the term probably refers to the defendant
in a legal trial who cannot afford to bribe the judge (i.e. Exod. 23:8; Deut. 16:19; Prov. 17:23; Isa. 1:23; 5:21; Jer. 5:28; Micah 3:11; 7:3)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: RIGHTEOUSNESS

▣ "And the needy for a pair of sandals" This may be interpreted literally as meaning

- people bought and sold for a very small amount (cf. Amos 8:5-6)

- a court procedure (i.e. the exchanging of shoes, cf. Ruth 4:7, see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel,
vol. 1, p. 169) to give some legality to these scandalous enslaving practices of the rich.

- The NET Bible, p. 1592, #24, mentions a possible textual emendation.

- נעלים ‒ BDB 653, "shoes"

- עלם ‒ KB 834 I, "hidden," referring to a bribe

The NIDOTTE, vol. 1, p. 228, has a significant statement related to the social concept
of "needy," "poor," and "poverty."

"Where western thinking stresses the economic aspect of poverty, the ANE
understood poverty in the context of shame and honor. So the possession of land, power,
economic security, and social states made a person rich, and the absence of these factors made a
person poor."

verses.zh: 他们见穷人头上所蒙的灰也都垂涎，阻碍谦卑人的道路。父子同一个女子行淫，亵渎我的圣名。
verses.en: They trample[NOTE:1] on the dirt-covered heads of the poor;[NOTE:2] they push the destitute away.[NOTE:3] A man and his father go to the same girl;[NOTE:4] in this way they show disrespect for[NOTE:5] my moral purity.[NOTE:6]
notes: Most scholars now understand this verb as derived from the root II שָׁאַף (shaʾaf, “to crush; to trample”), an alternate form of שׁוּף (shuf), rather than from I שָׁאַף (shaʾaf, “to pant, to gasp”; cf. KJV, ASV, NASB).

Heb “those who stomp on the dirt of the ground on the head of the poor.” It is possible to render the line as “they trample the heads of the poor into the dust of the ground,” thereby communicating that the poor are being stepped on in utter contempt (see S. M. Paul, Amos [Hermeneia], 79-80). The participial form הַשֹּׁאֲפִים (hashoʾafim) is substantival and stands in apposition to the pronominal suffix on מִכְרָם (mikhram, v. 6b).sn The picture of the poor having dirt-covered heads suggests their humiliation before their oppressors and/or their sorrow (see 2 Sam 1:2; 15:32).

Heb “they turn aside the way of the destitute.” Many interpreters take “way” to mean “just cause” and understand this as a direct reference to the rights of the destitute being ignored. The injustice done to the poor is certainly in view, but the statement is better taken as a word picture depicting the powerful rich pushing the “way of the poor” (i.e., their attempt to be treated justly) to the side. An even more vivid picture is given in Amos 5:12, where the rich are pictured as turning the poor away from the city gate (where legal decisions were made, and therefore where justice should be done).

Heb “go to the girl.” sn Most interpreters see some type of sexual immorality here (cf. KJV, NASB, NIV, NCV, NRSV, TEV, CEV, NLT), even though the Hebrew phrase הָלַךְ אֶל (halakh ʾel, “go to”) never refers elsewhere to sexual intercourse. (The usual idiom is בוֹא אֶל [boʾ ʾel]. However, S. M. Paul (Amos [Hermeneia], 82) attempts to develop a linguistic case for a sexual connotation here.) The precise identification of the “girl” in question is not clear. Some see the referent as a cultic prostitute (cf. NAB; v. 8 suggests a cultic setting), but the term נַעֲרָה (naʿarah) nowhere else refers to a prostitute. Because of the contextual emphasis on social oppression, some suggest the exploitation of a slave girl is in view. H. Barstad argues that the “girl” is the hostess at a pagan מַרְזֵחַ (marzeakh) banquet (described at some length in 6:4-7). In his view the sin described here is not sexual immorality, but idolatry (see H. Barstad, The Religious Polemics of Amos [VTSup], 33-36). In this case, one might translate, “Father and son go together to a pagan banquet.” In light of this cultic context, F. I. Andersen and D. N. Freedman argue that this is a reference to a specific female deity (“the Girl”) and correlate this verse with 8:14 (Amos [AB], 318-19).
Or “pollute”; “desecrate”; “dishonor.”
Heb “my holy name.” Here “name” is used metonymically for God’s moral character or reputation, while “holy” has a moral and ethical connotation.
verses.commentary:
2:7

NASB, NKJV
"pant"

NRSV, TEV, JPSOA
"trample"

NJB
"crushed"

REB
"grind"

LXX
"tread on"

Peshitta
"oppress"

There is much discussion about the translation of this term (BDB 983, KB 1375,
Qal ACTIVE PARTICIPLE) in Amos 2:7:

- the NASB and NKJV imply that the rich begrudged (i.e. "gasp for air" KB 1375 or "pant after"
BDB 983 I, e.g. Job 7:2; Ps. 119:131; Eccl. 1:5) the small amount of dust the poor placed on their
heads in mourning (hyperbole)

- the NRSV, following the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and JPSOA, translates this term "to crush" or "to trample"
(BDB 983 II, e.g. 8:4; Ps. 56:2; Ezek. 36:3), which seems to imply the affluent's humiliation
and domination of the poor.

In this context "the righteous," "the needy," "the helpless," and "the humble" refer not to
the perennially poor, but the recently exploited middle class farmers or merchants who had been forced
to borrow money and thereby lost their tribal lands, income, pride, and social position. For a good
discussion of the rich and poor in the OT see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, pp. 72-74. Because
of the term's use in Amos 8:4 the second option seems best.

▣

NASB, LXX
"turn aside the way of the humble"

NKJV
"pervert the way of the humble"

NRSV, REB
"push the afflicted out of the way"

TEV
"push the poor out of the way"

NJB
"thrust the rights of the oppressed to one side"

REB
"push the humble out of the way"

JPSOA
"make the humble walk a twisted course"

Peshitta
"turn away justice from the fatherless"

The VERB (BDB 639, KB 692, Hiphil IMPERFECT)
is used several times in Amos.

- In Amos 2:7 and 5:12 it refers to abuses of the legal system caused by the wealthy's
bribery of the judges (e.g. Exod. 23:6; Deut. 16:19; 24:17; 27:19; 1 Sam. 8:3; Prov. 17:23; Isa. 10:2; Lam. 3:35).

- In Amos 2:8 it refers to the wealthy reclining on the garments taken from the poor as pledges for a debt.

The basic meaning of the term is to "stretch out" or "spread out." In the first example above
the judges stretched out their hands for a bribe. In the second example the garments of the poor are spread out so
that the wealthy can sit on them or possibly lie on them, which could even imply cultic prostitution.

▣ "a man and his father resort to the same girl" The term for girl (BDB 655) here is not the normal
term for cult prostitute, although that may be what this is referring to (cf. Deut. 23:18; for historical setting see
Hosea 4:12-14). It could also refer to the "selling" of a poor, young maiden, whereby she would be used as a
concubine by all the men in one family (cf. TEV). This would violate

- Lev. 18:8; 20:11; Deut. 22:30; 27:20

- Exod. 21:7-11

Since the context is the abuse of the poor and helpless, then the second option seems best.

There have been several other interpretations (see NET Bible, p. 1593, #2). One cannot be specific
about the precise nature of some of these violations, but the overall context is very clear. Humans, even covenant people,
are sinful and violate God's laws! YHWH does not take sin and sinners lightly, especially those who should have known Him
(i.e. Judah and Israel, cf. Rom. 9:4-5). We reap what we sow in direct proportion to the light (and power) we have (see full list of texts at Gal. 6:7-10)!

▣ "In order to profane My holy name" These acts were flaunted at the shrines (golden calves
of Jeroboam II) at Bethel and Dan (cf. Amos 2:8). They had the appearance of legality and religious approval,
but everyone knew what was happening!

This VERBAL (BDB 320 III, KB 319, Piel INFINITIVE CONSTRUCT)
is used in several senses in the Piel form:

- to defile sexually, Lev. 19:29; 21:9,15

- to defile ceremonially, Lev. 19:8; 21:12,23; 22:9,15

- to defile YHWH's name, Lev. 18:21; 19:12; 20:3; 21:6; 22:2,32; Jer. 34:16; Ezek. 20:39; 36:20-23; Amos 2:7

The cultic acts of the Israelites were polluting, defiling, and profaning the very God
they claimed to worship and serve (cf. Ezek. 36:22-32)! They flagrantly ignored the Mosaic legislation for personal gain and pleasure!

It is obvious that Amos (like all of the prophets) judged actions in light of the Mosaic Law (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: PROPHECY [OT]).

- Amos 2:4 uses the terms "the law of the Lord" and "His
statutes" to refer to the Mosaic legislation (see SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS FOR GOD'S REVELATION).

- Amos 2:7 relates to Lev. 18:8,15; 20:11-12

- Amos 2:8 relates to Deut. 24:12-13

- Amos 2:9-11 relates to Gen. 15:12-21

- Amos 2:11-12 relates to Numbers 6

SPECIAL TOPIC: "THE NAME" OF YHWH (OT)

verses.zh: 他们在各坛旁铺人所当的衣服，卧在其上，又在他们神的庙中喝受罚之人的酒。
verses.en: They stretch out on clothing seized as collateral; they do so right[NOTE:1] beside every altar!They drink wine bought with the fines they have levied;they do so right in the temple[NOTE:2] of their God![NOTE:3]
notes: The words “They do so right” are supplied twice in the translation of this verse for clarification.
Heb “house.”

Or “gods.” The Hebrew term אֱלֹהֵיהֶם (ʾelohehem) may be translated “their gods” (referring to pagan gods), “their god” (referring to a pagan god, cf. NAB, NIV, NLT), or “their God” (referring to the God of Israel, cf. NASB, NRSV).
verses.commentary:
2:8 "On the garments taken as pledges they stretch out beside every altar" The rich were taking
and keeping (prohibited in Exod. 22:26-27; Deut. 24:12-13; Job 22:6) the sleeping garments (outer cloaks) of the poor
as a pledge for loans (see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 1, p. 171; cf. Exod. 21:7,26-28; Lev. 25:39-40;
Deut. 24:10-13,17; Prov. 20:16; 27:13). This may relate to cultic prostitution mentioned in Amos 2:7 or a cultic
meal connected to the worship of fertility gods.

The phrase, "every altar," shows the idolatrous nature of the worship being offered to Ba'al
(male) and Asherah (female), who were local fertility gods with an altar in each and every community. YHWH
had only one official altar (i.e. Mt. Moriah). Jeroboam I had established two alternate sites at Bethel and Dan to
prevent his people (i.e. the northern tribes) from returning to Jerusalem for feast days.

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE FEASTS OF ISRAEL

▣ "in the house of their God they drink the wine of those who have been fined" There are two possible interpretations:

- in the cultic centers of Dan and Bethel the rich were becoming intoxicated on the revenue
they illegally extracted from the poor

- the temple taxes were being used to promote drunkenness and sexual practices

Some translations translate Elohim as "their gods" or "their god"
(NJB, NAB, NIV), but the context implies a reference to YHWH (NASB, NRSV, TEV, JPSOA, NET). See
SPECIAL TOPIC: NAMES FOR DEITY,
C., D.

This is not a condemnation of wine, but of its abuse.

SPECIAL TOPIC: ALCOHOL AND ALCOHOLISM

verses.zh: 我从以色列人面前除灭亚摩利人。他虽高大如香柏树，坚固如橡树，我却上灭他的果子，下绝他的根本。
verses.en: For Israel’s sake I destroyed the Amorites.[NOTE:1] They were as tall as cedars[NOTE:2] and as strong as oaks,but I destroyed the fruit on their branches[NOTE:3] and their roots in the ground.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “I destroyed the Amorites from before them.” The translation takes מִפְּנֵי (mippeney) in the sense of “for the sake of.” See BDB 818 s.v. פָּנֻה II.6.a and H. W. Wolff, Joel and Amos (Hermeneia), 134. Another option is to take the phrase in a spatial sense, “I destroyed the Amorites, [clearing them out] from before them [i.e., Israel]” (cf. NIV, NRSV).
Heb “whose height was like the height of cedars.”
Heb “his fruit from above.”
Heb “and his roots from below.”
verses.commentary:
2:9-12 This is a historical rendition of the gracious acts of YHWH during the Conquest, which sets the stage for Israel's
judgment. God's people's violations of His covenant are not new, but perennial (cf. Nehemiah 9; Acts 7).

2:9 "it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them" This is "holy war" terminology referring to
YHWH fighting on behalf of His people (notice the FIRST PERSON SINGULAR PRONOUN
in Amos 2:9,10.13). The victory belonged to Him (e.g. "hornets," Exod. 23:28; Deut. 7:20; Josh. 24:12;
"hail stones," Josh. 10:11).

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMORITE

▣ "though his height" This may simply be imagery for power (BDB 147) using trees (cedars can grow up to
100' high; see SPECIAL TOPIC: TREES) or possibly a literal reference to the physical
height of some of the Amorites, Og of Bashan and the Anakim of Hebron (cf. Num.13:28, 33; Deut. 1:28; 9:2; Josh. 11:21-22).

SPECIAL TOPIC: TERMS USED FOR TALL/POWERFUL WARRIORS OR PEOPLE GROUPS

▣ "I even destroyed his fruit above and his root below" This is an idiom or proverb of total
destruction, here used of the Amorite people. Verses 9-10 draw imagery from the period of the Exodus and Conquest.

SPECIAL TOPIC: AMORITE

verses.zh: 我也将你们从埃及地领上来，在旷野引导你们四十年，使你们得亚摩利人之地为业。
verses.en: I brought you up from the land of Egypt;I led you through the wilderness for 40 yearsso you could take the Amorites’ land as your own.
verses.commentary:
2:10 "It was I who brought you up from the land of Egypt" The deliverance was prophesied to Abraham
(cf. Gen. 15:12-21). This special covenant relationship with the descendants of the Patriarchs is affirmed by
the national group in Exod. 19-20. But collectively they turned away and rejected YHWH's covenant (cf. Hosea 13:4-6).
Israel was more responsible because she had so much more spiritual light (cf. Rom. 9:4-5).

SPECIAL TOPIC: COVENANT PROMISES TO THE PATRIARCHS

▣ "I led you in the wilderness forty years" This is a reference to the wilderness wandering
period. The term "forty" is a round number in the OT. Here it refers to the thirty eight years of travel from
Kadesh-Barnea to the Promised Land (by way of the trans-Jordan).

SPECIAL TOPIC: THE EXODUS (uncertainties)

SPECIAL TOPIC: SYMBOLIC NUMBERS IN SCRIPTURE, #7

▣ "That you might take possession of the land of the Amorite" This refers to YHWH's
promise to Abraham in Gen. 15:12-21. Notice the term "Amorite" refers to

- all of the land of Canaan in Amos 2:16

- one of several indigenous tribes in Amos 2:21

SPECIAL TOPIC: PRE-ISRAELITE INHABITANTS OF PALESTINE

verses.zh: 我从你们子弟中兴起先知，又从你们少年人中兴起拿细耳人。以色列人哪，不是这样吗？这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: I made some of your sons prophetsand some of your young men Nazirites.[NOTE:1] Is this not true, you Israelites?”The Lord is speaking.
notes: Or perhaps “religious devotees” (also in the following verse). The Hebrew term נָזִיר (nazir) refers to one who is “consecrated” or “devoted” to God (see Num 6:1-21).
verses.commentary:
2:11-12 "I raised up some of your sons to be prophets. . .Nazirites" YHWH's special choice of these
spiritual leaders showed His special care for Israel. But Israel caused these men (and possibly women,
cf. Num. 6:2) to sin (cf. Amos 2:12). They were God's gift, but His people perverted their giftedness!

"Nazirites" are described in Numbers 6. They could be male or female (cf. Num. 6:2). There
were several unique guidelines for their calling to continue:

- cannot eat any product from the grapevine, Num. 6:3-4

- cannot cut his/her hair, Num. 6:5

- cannot touch a dead body (i.e. funerals of loved ones), Num. 6:6-7

This special vow (temporary [e.g. Num. 6:13-20; Acts 18:18; 21:23] or life long [Jdg.13:7;
1 Sam. 1:1; Luke 7:33]) was a way for people who were not priests or Levites to dedicate themselves to
YHWH in a special sense! It is also significant that in a male-dominated culture ancient Israelites allowed
female Nazirites (and prophetesses).

For a good brief discussion see Roland deVaux, Ancient Israel, vol. 2, pp. 466-467.

SPECIAL TOPIC: NAZIRITE VOW

SPECIAL TOPIC: WOMEN IN THE BIBLE

2:11 "Is this not so" YHWH challenges them to affirm the trustworthiness of His words of
condemnation. But this is also a sorrowful, personal message from their God! The phrase "sons of Israel"
has Abrahamic covenant implications. God still loves and cares for His people (His true people reflect His character!).

▣ "declares the Lord" This is a special phrase to denote God's
revelation (cf. Amos 2:11, 16; 3:10,13,15; 4:1,5-6, 8-11; 6:6, 14; 9:7-8,12,13).

verses.zh: 你们却给拿细耳人酒喝，嘱咐先知说：不要说预言。
verses.en: “But you made the Nazirites drink wine;[NOTE:1] you commanded the prophets, ‘Do not prophesy!’
notes: Nazirites were strictly forbidden to drink wine (Num 6:2-3).
verses.commentary:
2:12 The evil of God's people is exemplified by

- Nazirites ‒ drink

- prophets ‒ can not speak

This represents a total reversal in God's clearly revealed will for His people.

verses.zh: 看哪，在你们所住之地，我必压你们，如同装满禾捆的车压物一样。
verses.en: Look! I will press you down,like a cart loaded down with grain presses down.[NOTE:1]
notes: The precise meaning of this verse is unclear. Various suggested meanings have been proposed (see S. M. Paul, Amos [Hermeneia], 94). One option is to relate the verb to an Arabic verb meaning “to hinder; to hamper,” and translate, “I am making you immobile, like a cart filled with grain is immobile.” In this case, the Lord refers to Israel’s inability to escape his coming judgment (see vv. 14-16; NJPS). Another view relates the verb to a different Arabic verb, meaning “to cut in pieces.” The translation, “I will cut you in pieces as a cart cuts in pieces [the earth],” would refer to the ruts and rifts in the ground caused by an earthquake. Thirdly, some relate the verb to an Arabic root meaning “to groan,” with the idea that the Lord causes the ground underneath Israel to groan (cf. NLT). Fourth, the translation here connects the verb to an Aramaism signifying to “press down” (cf. NIV, NRSV). Lastly, some English versions translate the verb in an intransitive sense as “I am weighted down” (cf. NASB, NKJV), or “I groan beneath you” (NEB). For this last option, see F. I. Andersen and D. N. Freedman, Amos (AB), 334.
verses.commentary:
2:13 There are two ways to understand this verse.

- It refers to YHWH being weighed down (as an overloaded wagon) by His people's sin
(from Arabic root, cf. Isa. 43:24; and the NASB, NKJV, NET, NIV, REB translations).

- It refers to YHWH "pressing down" (i.e. judging) His people (from Arabic root, cf. Isa. 28:27-28;
and the NRSV, TEV, NJB).

- JPSOA

- in text, "I will slow your movements, as a wagon is slowed, when full of grain"

- in footnote, "I will slow your movements, as a threshing sledge is slowed, when clogged by cut grain"

The differences relate to which root the VERBS derive (BDB 734, KB 802,
Hiphil PARTICIPLE and Hiphil IMPERFECT). In this case certainty is impossible
(NET Bible gives four possible roots, p. 1593, #14).

The UBS, A Translator's Handbook on the Book of Amos, suggests a translation that follows
option #2, where the people of Israel groan under God's judgment like an overloaded cart, pp. 55-56. This series of grammar focused
information is very helpful. I commend it to you!

verses.zh: 快跑的不能逃脱；有力的不能用力；刚勇的也不能自救。
verses.en: Fast runners will find no place to hide;[NOTE:1] strong men will have no strength left;[NOTE:2] warriors will not be able to save their lives.
notes: Heb “and a place of refuge will perish from the swift.”
Heb “the strong will not increase his strength.”
verses.commentary:
2:14-16 This described the panicked retreat of the Israeli army before the Assyrians. YHWH had been
with them in the Exodus and Conquest, but now His presence was for judgment, not deliverance! He strikes
fear and panic into the hearts of Israel's best soldiers. This is an exact reversal of "Holy War"!

2:14,15

NASB, NJB, JPSOA
"life"

NKJV, REB, Peshitta
"himself"

NRSV, TEV
"lives"

LXX
"soul"

The MT has nephesh (BDB 659) which denotes a whole person.

Humans do not have a "soul" (i.e. Greek thought), they are a soul (Hebrew thought, cf. Gen. 2:7).

SPECIAL TOPIC: NEPHESH

verses.zh: 拿弓的不能站立；腿快的不能逃脱；骑马的也不能自救。
verses.en: Archers[NOTE:1] will not hold their ground;[NOTE:2] fast runners will not save their lives,nor will those who ride horses.[NOTE:3]
notes: Heb “the one who holds the bow.”

For the idiom of “holding [or “standing”] one’s ground” in battle, there is a similar phrase in Ezek 13:5; also related is the expression “to hold one’s own against” (or “to withstand”) in Judg 2:14; 2 Kgs 10:4; Dan 8:7 (see S. M. Paul, Amos [Hermeneia], 97). Other options include “will not endure” or “will not survive.”

The last two lines read literally, “The one fast in his feet will not rescue [his life], and the rider of the horse will not rescue his life.” The phrase “his life” does double duty in the parallelism and should be understood in both lines.

verses.zh: 到那日，勇士中最有胆量的，必赤身逃跑。这是耶和华说的。
verses.en: Bravehearted[NOTE:1] warriors will run away naked in that day.”The Lord is speaking.
notes: Or “the most stouthearted” (NAB); cf. NRSV “those who are stout of heart.”
verses.commentary:
2:16 "the warriors will flee naked" This idiomatic phrase refers to the throwing off of all armor
and all unnecessary clothing so that the soldiers could retreat even faster (JPSOA, "unarmed," but footnote, "naked").

▣ "in that day" This phrase, "in that day" or "on that day," is a way for the eighth century
prophets to speak of YHWH's visitation (presence), both for judgment and restoration (see
SPECIAL TOPIC: THAT DAY).

This pattern is typical of the prophets. God is going to act against sin in time, but
He also offers a day of repentance and forgiveness to those who change their hearts and actions! God's
purpose of redemption and restoration will be accomplished! He will have a people who reflect His
character. The purpose of creation (fellowship between YHWH and humanity) will be fulfilled (see SPECIAL TOPIC: Seek the Lord)!

SPECIAL TOPIC: REPENTANCE (OT)

FOLLOWING THE ORIGINAL AUTHOR'S INTENT AT PARAGRAPH LEVEL

This is a study guide commentary, which means that you are responsible for your own interpretation of the Bible.
Each of us must walk in the light we have. You, the Bible, and the Holy Spirit are priority in interpretation. You must not relinquish this to a commentator.

Read the chapter in one sitting. Identify the subjects (reading cycle #3). Compare your subject divisions with the five translations above. Paragraphing
is not inspired, but it is the key to following the original author's intent, which is the heart of interpretation. Every paragraph has one and only one subject.
